events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1 gives us no real mechanical information yet, so I’d rather not manufacture a confident read out of thin air. Early noise can help mafia hide as much as it helps town, so I’m watching for concrete reasoning, consistent vote intentions, and anyone trying to rush a conclusion before we have anything solid. I have no accusation right now and won’t force a yield.

Felix's framing matches my own: on Day 1 we're all guessing, so I'd rather build a record of who states what than pile onto a name with no support behind it. A couple of things I want to track as the discussion goes: whether people name specific behavior (vote patterns, who they lean on, inconsistencies) rather than vibes, and whether anyone claims special roles early. Right now nobody has, and I'm not going to invent a tell out of politeness. My own read is deliberately thin: I'm a plain villager with no investigation, no protection, and no way to verify anything, so my value is in voting honestly and in keeping the vote count honest rather than in pointing fingers confidently. If the poll today ends up tied or spread thin, I'd rather see people hold their votes than have a couple of loud voices manufacture a consensus out of a tie. I also want to say plainly that I won't be one of the people who reverse-engineers a mafia vote from the order of the night kill; the order tells us nothing about alignment. I'll update my suspicion only when someone gives a reason I can test against the next day's vote record.

I agree we shouldn't manufacture certainty, but with five votes needed for an elimination, a scattered vote can leave us with no elimination and less informative voting intentions. Arjun, when you say people should hold their votes in a tie or spread field, do you mean abstain even if they have a genuine suspicion?

To answer Sam directly, since Sam asked: no, I wasn't endorsing blanket abstention. My point was narrower — I don't want people to hold, or pile onto, a vote that exists only because a name is trending. If you have a genuine, testable suspicion about someone, you should vote for that person even in a spread field; abstaining to avoid 'manufacturing a consensus' is really just a way of letting the loudest voice set the agenda. Abstention, for me, is only right when you truly have no read at all, not as a general caution. And I'm not endorsing vote concentration for its own sake either — if five people converge on a name without reasons, that tells us less than five separate grounded reads that happen to land in different places.

On Sam's other point, that a scattered vote can mean no elimination: that's true, and it's the real tension. If the field is genuinely thin on day one, the honest outcome may be no elimination, and that costs us a day of information. I'd rather eat that cost than eliminate someone for a reason that turns out to be retroactive. The elimination threshold is a mechanic, not a reason.

So the record I want us to keep is: each of us states our current candidate and the specific thing that put them there. If I name someone tomorrow, it should be a behavior I can point to — a voting pattern, a claim of role, an inconsistency — not a vibe and not the shape of the discussion.

Sam, you framed this as the risk of a scattered vote with no elimination, and you've also been the one pushing for concrete reasoning over manufactured certainty. If the vote tonight is spread thin and one name leads on two votes while four others have one each, what do you think should happen — and would you hold your vote for the leading name on two votes alone, or would you want a stated reason attached before you join it?

Arjun, I wouldn't join a two-vote leader solely because they're leading. I'd want a reason I find more persuasive than the alternatives, and I'd state it before voting. That said, the threshold matters: if I have a comparable suspicion of the leader and someone unlikely to reach five, I may vote for the leader to make an elimination possible, while being honest about that tradeoff. A no-elimination day isn't automatically better just because our reads are uncertain.

Your clarification makes sense. I don't have a candidate yet; so far we've mostly discussed voting principles rather than alignment-indicative behavior. Also, since eliminated players' roles aren't revealed, even a completed vote won't confirm whether its target was mafia—we'll need to interpret the voting record cautiously.

The exchange between Arjun and Sam covers important theory on thresholds and abstention, but one detail in Arjun's opening post stood out to me: explicitly stating that he is a plain villager with no investigation or protection. Claiming vanilla unprompted on Day 1 doesn't help town. Even if completely true, narrowing the field of potential power roles early on only assists the mafia in their night-kill selection.

Regarding the broader discussion, I lean toward Sam's perspective on eliminations. With no role reveals upon death, we do have to be cautious about how we interpret flips, but walking away with a no-elimination day forfeits our primary town weapon while still giving the mafia a free night kill. We need voting data to analyze on future days. Right now, half the room hasn't spoken yet, so I want to hear where the rest of the table stands on candidates and Day 1 priorities before narrowing down a vote.

Kenji, directly: do you hold a power role yourself, and if you don't, on what basis do you think the table should discourage role disclosure on Day 1?

On the substance, I think the critique is aimed at the wrong target and misreads what I said. I didn't claim vanilla to buy cover; I stated a fact about my own action record — I have no investigation, no protection, and nothing to verify anyone with. That's disclosure of capability, not a strategic innocence claim. If I'm mafia, that sentence is worth nothing to me, because anyone can say it. So my claim doesn't narrow the pool of *possible* mafia for anyone who is actually reasoning about behavior; it only removes me from the set of people who might be holding a power role. Meanwhile, the real risk Kenji identifies — mafia getting free night-kill information — comes from the *power* roles being publicly identified, not from ordinary villagers saying they have no power. My argument in the first post was precisely that the detective and the doctor should stay quiet on Day 1, and I'd re-emphasize that rather than walk it back: the mafia's kill selection is the one place where knowing who has a gun and who has a shield matters most, and Day 1 is the cheapest possible night for them to learn it.

So if role claims are bad on Day 1, the coherent position is that nobody should volunteer *which* role they hold. Felix, Sam, and I haven't claimed anything beyond what's needed to state our reasoning. Kenji, you've criticized the shape of my statement while not stating your own role or your own candidate — and you've noted that half the room hasn't spoken yet. That's a reasonable sequencing point, but I'd like to know whether your objection is about disclosure in general or specifically about me, because the answer changes my read. If it's general, I'll support keeping the detective and the doctor silent. If it's specifically about me, I'd want the behavioral reason attached, not a preference for how the table should talk.

My candidate list is still empty, and I'm not going to manufacture one from a disagreement about meta-conventions. That's not a vote for Kenji — I have no read on him beyond the fact that he moved first against a specific claim without offering one of his own, which I'll note and revisit once we have a voting record to test it against. I'll be the first to say a convention dispute is thin material; that's why I'm asking the question instead of drafting the name.

Arjun, asking me directly whether I hold a power role is completely backwards and demonstrates exactly why your initial disclosure was problematic. Town members should never be pressured into confirming or denying power roles on Day 1. Answering that question only benefits the mafia by narrowing down where the detective and doctor might be.

To address your question directly: my objection is rooted in a general principle that specifically applies to your action because you were the one who volunteered the claim. The logic isn't complicated. If multiple villagers publicly declare they have no investigative or protective capabilities, the mafia doesn't need absolute trust in those claims to gain an informational edge; it systematically shrinks the pool of candidates when they make their night-kill decisions. Advocating that power roles remain silent while villagers claim vanilla misses the point entirely—villagers staying silent is what protects the power roles by keeping them hidden within the full group.

You have now exhausted all three of your speaking turns for Day 1, so the back-and-forth between us has run its course. I want to see where Noah, Lucia, Isha, Zara, and Amara stand, as over half the table has yet to speak. I will not yield, allowing the poll to bring new voices into the discussion.

I'm Amara, and I'll keep this about behavior rather than role claims. Arjun has now used his three turns, which Kenji is right about, but the question Arjun asked Kenji still stands. My concern is Kenji's handling of Arjun's disclosure. Kenji called Arjun's no-power-role statement a problem, then argued that villagers should stay silent about roles because silence protects power roles. Those two positions pull against each other. Kenji's objection was aimed at the one player who had answered him directly, while Felix and Sam, who also have not claimed roles, were not asked to stay quiet. After that, Kenji declined to yield and said the poll should bring in new voices. That is a pattern I want to test. Does Kenji apply the disclosure convention evenly, or only to Arjun? My read on Kenji is thin but specific, and I am not voting on it today. Kenji, directly: if a villager stating no power role actually helps mafia target people, why did you single out Arjun instead of asking Felix and Sam to stay silent too?

Amara, your question rests on a complete misreading of both the thread and my argument. I never said villagers should stay silent in the game; I said players should remain silent about their roles. Arjun was the only person at the table who unprompted declared himself a plain villager with no power role. Felix and Sam never claimed or disclosed anything about their roles. Why would I reprimand Felix or Sam for role disclosure when neither of them disclosed a role? Furthermore, claiming that criticizing a vanilla claim and arguing that villagers should not disclose roles pull against each other makes no sense—they are the exact same principle. Pointing out that narrowing the pool of unconfirmed roles aids the mafia is standard town play. Manufacturing a contradiction where none exists and faulting me for not scolding players who did nothing wrong looks like an opportunistic attempt to cast shade. This is my third and final turn for Day 1, so I cannot speak again today. We still need to hear from Noah, Lucia, Isha, and Zara, none of whom have spoken yet. I am setting yield to null so the poll can finally bring the rest of the town into the discussion.

First time speaking, so let me give my take on the thread that's dominated Day 1.

I think Kenji's core principle is right: nobody should volunteer which specific role they hold, on Day 1 or ever, voluntarily. Arjun's disclosure — even if true and even if made in good faith — does narrow the pool of potential power roles for anyone reasoning about it. The more players who confirm vanilla status, the more the remaining unclaimed names draw attention from the mafia's night kill. The correct convention is silence on roles from everyone.

That said, I want to address Amara's push directly, because I think it's worth separating what Kenji actually said from what was attributed to him. Amara framed Kenji's objection as selectively targeting Arjun while ignoring Felix and Sam — but Kenji's response is simply accurate: only Arjun made a role claim. There was no disclosure to criticize from the others. If Amara's read on Kenji is that his objection was opportunistic rather than principled, I'd want that grounded in a behavior beyond what he's said in this thread. Right now his position — don't disclose roles because it helps the mafia — is coherent and doesn't depend on having a power role himself.

Amara, I want to ask you directly: when you identified the supposed contradiction in Kenji's positions, was that a reading of what he actually said, or a reading of what you expected him to say? Because the two positions you described pull against each other only if Kenji had also told villagers to stay silent — and he didn't. That distinction matters for whether your push is a genuine town read or a way to put early pressure on a vocal player.

Noah, fair challenge, and I'll answer directly. I wrote that Kenji's positions 'pull against each other,' but that was my reading of his push rather than a sentence where he told villagers to stay silent. Kenji's e9 did say villagers staying silent protects power roles, and his e11 separates players staying silent about roles from villagers being silent, so his two objections fit one principle. I withdraw the contradiction claim as I wrote it. What I still see is narrower and sits on the record. Arjun asked Kenji directly whether he holds a power role, and Kenji answered with a principle rather than a yes or no. I asked why he singled out Arjun instead of Felix and Sam, and he replied that Felix and Sam never disclosed roles. That is a fair factual point, but he did not address whether his objection applies to anyone who volunteers vanilla status. Kenji has now used all three turns without stating his own role or any candidate. I'm not voting on that today. It's a pattern to track: whether he answers direct questions when they cut against his own position. Felix and Sam, you haven't claimed a role. Do you read Arjun's statement as a role claim, or as a capability statement? Lucia, Isha, and Zara, you haven't spoken yet, and I'd like your read on Day 1 priorities, including whether a no-elimination day is acceptable.

Amara, I read Arjun’s statement as a capability statement, not a role claim. It tells us he says he has no investigation or protection; it does not tell us alignment, and I don’t think it’s vote-worthy on its own. I also think your correction on the supposed contradiction was fair: Kenji’s principle is coherent as long as it applies to role disclosure, and only Arjun disclosed anything. That exchange has used a lot of Day 1 oxygen without giving me a candidate. I’m not going to manufacture one from meta-conventions, and I’m not voting Kenji or Arjun over it. What I want now is concrete vote intentions and the remaining voices. Lucia, Isha, and Zara haven’t spoken, and I want to hear whether any of them sees an actual behavioral suspect rather than a disclosure dispute. My current candidate list is empty.

Noah, you asked for my read on Day 1 priorities, so here it is. I'm a villager with no candidate yet. I'd rather not eliminate someone on a thin read, but a no-elimination day shouldn't become the default either, because it gives mafia a free night. Five votes are needed to eliminate, so a leader on two or three votes with reasons attached is more useful than a bandwagon. I don't want to spend more Day 1 on the Arjun and Kenji disagreement. Both sides have stated their positions, and I'd rather we track behavior, such as who votes consistently and who answers direct questions when they cut against their own position. Isha, you haven't spoken yet, and you're the only one of the remaining players I haven't heard from. Do you have an actual behavioral suspect, and if so, what is it based on?

Lucia, direct answer to your question: no, I don't have a behavioral suspect yet, and I want to be honest about that rather than manufacture one to seem engaged. What I've been doing is tracking who's pushed concrete claims versus who's argued meta-conventions, and the record so far is mostly the latter.

A few observations I want on the record:

Arjun's vanilla disclosure was a mistake on his part — not because it was a strategic claim, but because it gave Kenji something to attack instead of an actual alignment tell to evaluate. Kenji was right that role disclosure on Day 1 helps the mafia regardless of intent. The fact that this consumed four speaking turns (two from each) without producing a single candidate is itself informative — we spent our most productive early real estate on a convention dispute.

Amara's initial contradiction claim against Kenji was genuinely misread, and she was right to withdraw it. But the narrowing of her attack — 'he didn't answer the yes-or-no' — is worth noting. Arjun asked Kenji to confirm or deny a power role, which is itself the exact kind of question town should not pressure into. Amara later reframed it as a fair principle question, but the original ask wasn't one.

Noah's defense of Kenji in e12 was fair on the facts but did select the most charitable reading of Kenji while asking Amara to justify hers. That asymmetry isn't mafia-indicative on its own — Noah may genuinely read it that way — but I'd rather see Noah apply the same charitable standard to both sides consistently going forward.

Right now my honest state is: no candidate, no vote target, and I'd rather hear Zara speak before I commit to anything. The voting record tonight will be more informative than anything else we say in discussion.

Lucia, I accept the point that my attack narrowed. My e10 question was whether Kenji applies the disclosure rule evenly, and my e13 concern is a pattern to track, not a verdict. Two things are on the record. First, when Arjun asked Kenji directly whether he holds a power role, Kenji answered with a principle instead of a yes or no. Second, Kenji has used all three turns without stating his own role or any candidate. Noah, your charitable reading of Kenji is fair, but I'd like the same standard applied to Kenji's non-answers that you applied to my question. Zara, you're the last player who hasn't spoken. Do you see Kenji's refusal to answer directly as a behavioral concern, or as part of a Day 1 convention dispute? I'm not voting on Kenji today. If I vote for anyone tomorrow, it will be for a reason I can test against the vote record.

Since I'm the last voice to arrive, let me give my read on what Day 1 has actually produced rather than re-litigating it. Amara asked whether I see Kenji's non-answers as a behavioral concern or a convention dispute, so I'll answer that directly: I see it as mostly convention dispute. The disclosure argument took up a lot of our time, but both sides' positions were internally consistent by the end. Kenji's objection was aimed at an actual disclosure, and his refusal to confirm or deny a power role is the correct behavior regardless of alignment — nobody should be answering that question, so I won't treat the non-answer as a tell. Arjun's vanilla statement was a mistake in hindsight, but it reads to me as clumsy transparency, not misdirection; anyone could make that claim, which is exactly why it carries little signal either way. Amara's withdrawal of the contradiction claim was clean, and I'd rather judge people by how they handle corrections than by their first draft. Lucia's point about tracking who answers questions when it costs them is the right metric going forward — that's something the vote record and tomorrow's discussion can actually test. On the elimination question, I side with Sam and Lucia: a no-elimination day is acceptable if reads are genuinely thin, but I don't want it to become the comfortable default, because the mafia gets a free night either way and we lose our one source of hard data. My candidate list is empty right now, and I won't manufacture one from a meta dispute. If a name leads tonight with reasons attached rather than momentum, I'll vote for it; if the field stays scattered, I'll abstain and take the information loss deliberately.

My weakest suspicion is Amara. She corrected her initial misreading, which I appreciate, but then continued to flag Kenji for not answering whether he held a power role and for not stating his own role. Refusing to disclose that information is consistent with the principle Kenji stated, not a meaningful non-answer.

That is a thin behavioral concern, not proof of alignment. I’m not committed to voting for her, but I wanted to put a specific read on the record rather than leave my candidate list empty. I’ll weigh any other stated reasons before voting; I won’t join a leader merely because they’re leading.

Sam's read on Amara is the first concrete candidate anyone has put on the table today, and I want to sit with it before the vote. It's thin — and Sam acknowledges that — but it's specific: Amara corrected her contradiction claim, then kept pressing Kenji on non-answers after Kenji had already invoked the principle that nobody should confirm or deny a power role. The pattern of narrowing an attack but not dropping it is worth noting. I'm not saying Amara is mafia; I'm saying it's the kind of behavioral observation the rest of us should be producing more of instead of spending another turn on disclosure conventions.

What I notice across the full record: Arjun and Kenji are both out of turns, Amara is on her third, and we still have no one with a strong candidate. Sam has weak suspicion on Amara. Everyone else lists an empty candidate field. That's honest, but it's also the exact conditions where a no-elimination day becomes inevitable — and I share Felix and Lucia's concern that letting that become comfortable costs us a night and a data point.

My stance: I will not vote for a name solely because it leads, but I also won't hide behind 'reads are thin' if I have a real concern by the time votes are called. If anyone has a genuine suspicion — even a weak one — now is the time to put it on the record so the rest of us can weigh it against vote intentions tonight.

Felix, you've spoken twice and your candidate list remains empty. With three of us done with our turns and the vote approaching, do you have any suspicion at all — even weakest-level — that you'd be willing to state? You don't need to name a vote target, just a name and a reason, so the rest of us know where you stand when we're deciding ours.

Noah, direct answer: my weakest suspicion is Amara. It isn't strong, and I won't pretend otherwise. What stands out is that after she withdrew the contradiction claim, she kept framing Kenji's refusal to confirm or deny a power role as a behavioral concern. That refusal is exactly what a town player should do under Kenji's stated principle, and Amara herself acknowledged the principle was coherent. Continuing to press it as a pattern feels like narrowing an accusation after the original basis was removed. That said, I don't think it's enough to call her mafia, and I won't vote her merely because she's a name on the board. I'd weigh other stated reasons and the vote record. I also agree with Lucia and Zara that a no-elimination day should not be the default, but I won't manufacture certainty from this. Right now my candidate list contains only Amara as a weak note; everyone else is empty for me. If the final vote is between a thin but reasoned candidate and abstention, I'd prefer the reasoned vote, but I want the reason attached, not momentum.

This is my third and final turn, so let me put my card on the table and then hand off.

Two players — Sam and Felix — have independently named Amara as their weakest suspicion, and both flagged the same pattern: Amara withdrew her contradiction claim against Kenji but kept pressing him on not answering direct questions about his role. I want to weigh in on that before votes are called.

I don't think the pattern is inherently suspicious. Pressing someone who won't answer a direct question is standard town behavior — if anything, the concern would be if someone *stopped* pressing after raising an issue, because that looks more like a probe that served its purpose than genuine suspicion. Amara's continued pressure could equally be a town player who genuinely finds non-answers unsettling. Two people converging on the same weak read is worth noting, but it's also exactly the kind of momentum-driven convergence we've all agreed not to follow blindly.

What I want to flag instead is something structural: we've spent nearly all of Day 1 on the Arjun-Kenji disclosure dispute and Amara's follow-up, and the result is a field where everyone lists either an empty candidate or a weak one. That's honest, but it means tonight's vote is where the real information lives. I'd rather see five or six people state a candidate with a reason — even a weak one — than see four abstentions and three votes on Amara simply because she's the only name anyone has produced.

My own candidate list: I have no strong suspicion of anyone at the table based on behavioral evidence alone. If I'm voting tonight, it will be because a reason stated in the last hour before votes convinces me — not because a name is circulating.

Zara, you've only spoken once, and you gave what I thought was the most balanced read of the day — distinguishing convention dispute from behavioral concern. With the vote hours away and only you, Lucia, and Isha still having turns, I want to ask you directly: of everyone who's spoken, is there anyone whose *handling of a correction or challenge* — not their stated positions — registered as off to you? You said you judge people by how they handle corrections; has anyone handled one poorly enough to move your needle?

Noah, since you asked me directly: no, nobody's handling of a correction has moved my needle enough to name a strong suspect. Arjun's vanilla statement reads to me as clumsy transparency, and his follow-up defense was coherent even if the convention dispute itself was a poor use of the day. Kenji's refusal to confirm or deny a power role is correct behavior under the principle he stated, so I don't treat it as a non-answer. Amara's withdrawal was clean, and I said so earlier — I still think withdrawing a misread quickly is a point in her favor, not against her.

That said, I'll be honest about the one concrete thing on the table. Sam and Felix independently flagged the same narrow pattern: Amara accepted that the contradiction claim failed, but kept pressing Kenji's refusal to answer a role question as a behavioral concern, after herself acknowledging the principle was coherent. That's not damning — continued pressure on non-answers is often exactly what town should do. But it is the only specific, testable behavioral observation anyone has produced today, and everything else in the record is empty candidate lists or convention theory. So Amara sits as my weakest note too, for that stated reason and nothing else. I will not vote a name into a lead on that alone, and I'd say the same if the note were attached to anyone else at the table.

On the elimination question, my position hasn't changed from my first turn: no-elimination is acceptable if reads are genuinely thin, but I don't want it to become the comfortable default. If tonight's field produces a leader with reasons attached rather than momentum, I'll weigh it honestly. If it stays scattered with no reasons, I'll abstain deliberately and take the information loss.

One thing I want to flag before the vote: three of us have now independently landed on Amara as a weak note. That convergence is worth treating carefully — it could reflect a real shared observation, or it could just be the path of least resistance once a name exists. Everyone here has said they don't follow momentum, so tonight is where we find out whether that was sincere.

Lucia, one direct question, since you said you'd be watching whether charitable standards get applied consistently: does the convergence of three separate players on the same weak Amara note change your read of her, or do you treat repeated independent observations as more credible than a single one? I'm asking because your answer determines whether this is a genuine signal or an artifact, and I'd rather know before votes are called.

Zara, direct answer: repeated observations count for more than a single one only when they are independent. I count two flags on Amara, from Sam and then Felix, and Felix's note followed Sam's framing closely, so I'd treat it as one and a half. Noah explicitly said the pattern is not inherently suspicious, and your own note is the same weak read, not a third independent one. So the convergence is real but thin. It moves my read on Amara from empty to weak, not to a vote. Her pattern is that she kept pressing Kenji's refusal after conceding the contradiction. That is testable but not damning, since pressing a non-answer is ordinary town behavior. Isha's point that Noah applied charity asymmetrically is also worth tracking. Noah's answer to Amara was fair, but he asked her to justify her view without asking the same of Kenji's non-answers. I won't vote on any of this alone. My current plan is to abstain unless someone gives a reason that holds up on a second read. Felix and Sam, your Amara notes would be more useful if you could say whether they would still stand if the Kenji dispute were removed from the thread, because that would show whether the concern is about her behavior or about one exchange.

Lucia, your independence analysis on the Amara convergence is the sharpest read today. You're right that Felix following Sam's framing isn't a separate observation, and Noah explicitly said the pattern isn't inherently suspicious — so his note isn't a third vote either. That leaves two players with essentially one shared observation.

On the Amara note itself: pressing a non-answer after withdrawing a broader claim is ambiguous. Town does it when they genuinely find non-answers unsettling; mafia does it when they need to keep pressure alive after an original angle collapsed. The behavior alone doesn't discriminate between alignments.

My honest state: no candidate strong enough to vote on. My weakest note sits on Noah — the asymmetry I flagged earlier, where he asked Amara to justify her view while accepting Kenji's position without applying the same scrutiny. Not enough to vote him, but it's the only specific thing I'd track going forward.

You said you'd abstain unless a reason holds up on a second read. If tonight comes down to Amara on thin flags versus a scattered field with no leader, which outcome gives us more to work with tomorrow?

Isha, direct answer. A thin Amara vote is the worse outcome right now, though only narrowly. Roles are not revealed on death, so an elimination tells us almost nothing about alignment beyond the voting record. If we eliminate on flags that even their own sponsors describe as weak, and Amara is town, we lose a townie, gain little information, and the mafia keeps their night kill either way. A no-elimination day costs us a night, but it keeps the same field for Day 2, when we can test the current notes against new behavior. My preference is to hold unless someone brings a reason that survives a second read. That is my honest position, and it is not a vote for anyone. On the record: my candidate list is still empty. My only note is the pattern on Amara that Sam and Felix raised, which Noah correctly said is not inherently suspicious. I don't count it as a vote. I also don't want a no-elimination day to become automatic. If a leader emerges with reasons attached, I'll weigh it honestly, and since five votes are needed, a leader would need real support. I agree with Isha that Noah's answer to Amara asked more of her than it asked of Kenji's non-answers. I don't think that is mafia-indicative on its own, so I'm not building a case on it. Zara, you have not yet spoken on Amara directly. You called the convergence on her a path-of-least-resistance risk and said the note is the only testable observation on the table. If Amara is the only name tonight, would you vote for her, abstain, or hold, and what specific reason would move you?

Lucia, you asked me directly, so here's my direct answer: if Amara is the only name on the board tonight, I abstain. I won't vote her, and I won't treat a thin note as a reason to eliminate.

The reasoning is the same one you laid out yourself. Every sponsor of the Amara note — Sam, Felix, Noah, and me — has described it as weak, and Noah explicitly said the underlying pattern is not inherently suspicious. Pressing a non-answer is ordinary town behavior. On top of that, roles are not revealed on elimination, so removing Amara on these flags would cost us a town player and tell us almost nothing beyond the vote record itself. A no-elimination day costs us a night; a wrong elimination costs us a player and buys us nearly nothing. That trade is bad, and I don't think it becomes better just because a name is the only one circulating.

What would actually move my needle on Amara: a stated reason that survives a second read independent of the Kenji exchange. Lucia asked Felix and Sam exactly the right question — whether the note stands if the disclosure dispute is removed from the thread. If their answer is no, then there is no case at all, just one argument wearing a name. If their answer is yes, I want to hear what the residual behavior is, stated specifically enough that Day 2's vote record can test it. I'd also move if Amara's own stated positions start contradicting each other in a way that isn't a misreading she owns up to — she handled her first correction cleanly, which I still count in her favor.

To be clear about my own consistency: I put Amara down as my weakest note, and I stand by that as a note, not a vote. A weak note means 'track this,' not 'eliminate this.' Converting the first name anyone produced into an elimination just because it's first is exactly the path-of-least-resistance outcome I warned about earlier, and I'd say the same if the name were anyone else's.

On the broader picture: we're likely heading toward either a scattered field or a thin Amara leader. If it's scattered, I take the information loss deliberately. If Amara somehow reaches five votes, the record of who joined and why will be tomorrow's most valuable data either way.

Isha, one direct question, since you're the other player with turns left and you put a note on Noah rather than Amara: your asymmetry read — that Noah scrutinized Amara's challenge more than Kenji's non-answers — would it still stand if the Amara thread had never happened, or is it only visible against the background of that exchange? I'm asking for the same reason Lucia asked Felix and Sam: I want to know whether your note is about Noah's behavior or about one argument, because that determines whether it's trackable on Day 2 or just residue from today's dispute.

Zara, direct answer to your question: it's both. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
